    3. Policy rate, effective rate and real rate
    • Macroeconomics

    Policy rate, effective rate and real rate

    The Fed does not set a single interest rate but a target range. The rate banks actually pay, the effective rate, forms inside that range. The real rate shows how far the rate is above or below inflation: inflation is subtracted because what money really earns is measured in purchasing power, which shrinks as prices rise.

    What is the target range?

    The Fed's policy committee (FOMC) sets a target range for the rate banks charge each other on overnight loans, for example 5.25–5.50%. The range is 25 basis points (0.25 points) wide and at each meeting it can stay the same, go up or go down.

    The target range is a decision, not a single market rate. "The Fed rate" usually means this range or its upper bound.

    What is the effective rate?

    The effective federal funds rate is the average of the rates banks actually paid that day on overnight loans; the New York Fed publishes it every business day. With its tools, the Fed keeps this rate inside the target range, so it usually sits a little above the middle of it; for example about 5.33% while the range is 5.25–5.50%.

    In short, the target range is the decided rate and the effective rate the actual one. They differ by only a few basis points.

    What is the real rate, and why subtract inflation?

    An interest rate tells how much money grows in a year. But if prices rise in the same year, what that money can buy does not grow as much. The real rate is the difference: real rate ≈ interest rate − inflation.

    Example (round numbers): money kept for a year at 5.3% becomes 105.3 instead of 100. If prices rose 3.4% that year, a basket that cost 100 now costs 103.4. The real gain in purchasing power is about 1.9%. With inflation at 8.6% and the rate at 1.6%, the money would still grow in nominal terms but its purchasing power would fall by about 7%: a negative real rate.

    That is why a rate read on its own can mislead. A 5% rate with 2% inflation can mean tight policy; with 9% inflation, loose policy.

    How is it read?

    • Positive real rate: the rate is above inflation. Policy is often read as tight (slowing demand).
    • Negative real rate: the rate is below inflation. Policy is often read as loose (supportive); the purchasing power of saved money erodes.
    • Near zero: the rate and inflation are close; policy is seen as neither clearly tight nor clearly loose.
    • These readings are tendencies. The economy's "neutral" rate is not known exactly; the same real rate can work differently in different periods.

    Which inflation, which period?

    A real rate can be worked out in two ways. Backward-looking, with the latest released inflation (rate − latest CPI). Forward-looking, with the market's expected inflation; in the bond market its measure is the yield on inflation-protected bonds (TIPS).

    The real rate on the site's "Fed and inflation" card is backward-looking: the month's average effective rate minus the latest CPI (year on year) released by then. A CPI release describes the month before. It is a simple difference, not a forecast or an assessment.

    The same rate, different pictures

    Example periods (rounded figures).

    Mid-2022

    Effective rate about 1.2% (June average), CPI about 8.6%. Real rate about −7.4%. The Fed had started raising, but the rate was far below inflation.

    Early 2024

    Effective rate about 5.3%, CPI about 3.4%. Real rate about +1.9%. The rate was clearly above inflation.

    Rate unchanged, inflation moving

    Even if the Fed never moves, the real rate rises as inflation falls; policy tightens by itself.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • How far the rate is above or below inflation
    • The link between the decided range and the rate that actually forms
    • A rough sign of whether policy is tight or loose

    What it does not prove

    • What the Fed will do at its next meeting
    • Where inflation will go
    • Which way asset prices will move

    Often confused with

    • Fed rate decisions (FOMC)On decision day the Fed announces the target range; the effective rate forms inside it in the days after.
    • Real rates and the dollarThe real rate on the gold page is usually the 10-year TIPS yield (forward-looking, long term); this page is about the backward-looking gap of the short-term policy rate.

    Key points

    • The Fed sets a target range (e.g. 5.25–5.50%); the effective rate is what banks actually pay and sits inside it.
    • Real rate ≈ rate − inflation; it describes the real change in purchasing power.
    • A positive real rate is often read as tight, a negative one as loose policy.
    • The site's real rate is backward-looking (effective rate − latest released CPI); it is not a forecast.
